card.hook: Marienplatz is the kind of square where you spend ten minutes dodging strangers' elbows, then climb about 300 steps and suddenly have the whole thing to yourself, laid out below like a model village.
card.stand_here: Climb Alter Peter, the tower of St. Peter's Church at Rindermarkt 1, and stand on the viewing platform at 56 m. It's about 1 minute on foot south of Mary's Column, and from the platform you face north over the square, with the New Town Hall across from you and the Frauenkirche domes behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole square in one go. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the Frauenkirche domes, the golden figure on the column or the town hall tower, and 0.5x if you want more rooftops and streets.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put Mary's Column near a crossing point and let the New Town Hall fill the top of the frame, keeping your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day if you want the Alps showing in the distance. The square gets packed around the Glockenspiel shows at 11 am and noon (and 5 pm from March to October), so ground-level shots are easier outside those times.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the Fischbrunnen (Fish Fountain) in front of the New Town Hall, use the front camera and turn so the town hall facade fills the background over your shoulder. For something quieter, try the inner courtyard behind the Glockenspiel, where the clock tower and spiral staircases make a great backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the south side of the square while you stand near Mary's Column in the middle, with the New Town Hall facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Alter Peter tower is a ticketed climb up stairs, so check the official site for times and entry details before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the golden Virgin on top of Mary's Column, then head down and find all four little putti at its base.
card.good_to_know: Marienplatz has been Munich's main square since 1158. Mary's Column went up in 1638 to mark the end of the Swedish occupation, and the golden Virgin on top is a statue made in 1590 that once stood in the Frauenkirche. The four putti at the base each fight a different beast, standing for war, pestilence, hunger and heresy.

card.hook: The Residenz has ten courtyards and 130 rooms, so trying to squeeze it all into one photo is a losing game. Pick one side, make it the star, and you'll come away with a much better shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Hofgarten, on the long central allee, and look towards the Dianatempel. The Residenz is to the south-west of this point, so turn that way to see the garden-facing wing.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the temple framed by the garden paths, then try 2x to pull it closer to the flowerbeds. Over on Max-Joseph-Platz, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit more of the long front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the allee in the middle, and put some flowers low in the frame so the paths lead the eye to the temple.
card.best_time: Spring and summer are best, when the beds around the temple are in bloom.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Hofgarten on the palace's north side and turn so the Residenz facade is behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x if you want more of the palace over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Residenzstraße, near the Odeonsplatz end, to take your photo with the Residenz front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Hofgarten is free to enter and open daily, but the palace interior and courtyards are ticketed, so check the official site first. Photography isn't permitted in the Treasury (Schatzkammer).
card.challenge: Can you get the twin towers of the Theatine Church peeking out behind the garden wing without cutting off the flowers at the bottom?
card.good_to_know: The Residenz was the royal palace of the Wittelsbach rulers of Bavaria, and it's the largest city palace in Germany. It grew over more than four centuries from a fortress begun in 1385, so you'll spot Renaissance, Baroque, Rococo and Neo-Classical styles. The Königsbau on Max-Joseph-Platz was built for Ludwig I between 1825 and 1835, in the style of the Palazzo Pitti in Florence.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Hofgarten, on the long central allee, and look towards the Dianatempel. The Residenz is to the south-west of this point, so turn that way to see the garden-facing wing.

card.hook: Watch Platzl for two minutes and you'll see the same dance: people shuffling backwards with their phones up, trying to fit a whole beer hall in the frame. Join in, because the square gives you just enough room.
card.stand_here: Stand on Platzl, on the Orlandohaus side of the square where Orlandostraße runs in, with the building just to the south, about 1 minute on foot. Face the Hofbräuhaus across the open space, with the Orlandohaus beside it at the edge of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole facade. If it won't all fit, tap 0.5x and keep the phone level so the edges don't lean in. Use zoom 2x for the entrance and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines, then tap the building and slide it a touch darker if the sky is washing out the facade.
card.best_time: Early morning, when the light on the square is soft. Take a few frames while people move through and pick the cleanest.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Platzl right in front of the main facade at Platzl 9. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the Hofbräuhaus sits over your shoulder. It's always crowded here, so be patient and grab a few frames.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Pfisterstraße end of Platzl, looking across the square toward the Hofbräuhaus, while you pose in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Platzl is busy with pedestrians and traffic most of the time, so keep an eye on your surroundings while you frame your shot. Inside, the hall is crowded and people may not want to be photographed, so ask first.
card.challenge: Get the whole facade and a slice of the Orlandohaus in one straight-edged shot, with nobody's head blocking the door.
card.good_to_know: The first building here dates from 1589, when Duke Maximilian I had it built as an extension of the court brewery. Ordinary members of the public were let in from 1828. Most of it was destroyed in the Second World War, apart from the old beer hall (the Schwemme), and it was carefully rebuilt by 1958.

card.hook: The Frauenkirche is so tall that your phone can't take it all in at first, and the two round domes on top look like a pair of bald heads peeking over the Old Town. Locals just call it the Frauenkirche, and you'll spot those domes from across the city.
card.stand_here: Stand in Frauenplatz, the square right beside the cathedral, and face the red brick façade so both towers are straight ahead of you. Keep the phone upright and level instead of tilting it up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because at 1x you won't fit the whole church in from this close. Then try 1x, or 2x to 5x if your phone has them, to home in on the brickwork or the domes.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the brickwork looks warm and the square is quieter.
card.selfie_here: Stand in Frauenplatz in front of the main entrance with the twin towers behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your arm out so the towers rise over your shoulder. It's a classic photo spot, so check on the ground that it works for you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner of Liebfrauenstraße and Schäfflerstraße while you pose with the cathedral's two towers behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the cathedral, flash and selfie sticks aren't allowed, and visitors are asked to use a smartphone. The south tower is a separate visit, so check the official site for visiting times and tower access.
card.challenge: Get both towers dead straight on the gridlines, then take a second shot with your face in the corner and the towers still perfectly upright.
card.good_to_know: Work began in 1468 and the church was consecrated in 1494. The towers are just over 98 metres tall and got their domes in 1525. Tall Gothic spires were planned but never built because the money ran out.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Frauenplatz, the square right beside the cathedral, and face the red brick façade so both towers are straight ahead of you. Keep the phone upright and level instead of tilting it up.

card.hook: About 300 steps up a church tower, and suddenly the whole of Viktualienmarkt is laid out below you: rows of stalls, the maypole, and the old-town towers behind. Your legs will complain, but the photo is worth it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the observation deck of Alter Peter, the tower of St. Peter's Church, at the foot of Petersbergl in the old town. Face out over the market so the stalls and maypole are below you and the New Town Hall and Frauenkirche are in the wider view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole market in. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the New Town Hall or the Frauenkirche. Once you're down among the stalls, zoom 0.5x fits in a whole row of them plus the maypole.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the stalls in the lower part of the frame, with the old-town towers above them.
card.best_time: Go on a day when the market is trading, because the stalls are closed on Sundays and holidays. Morning or midday, when the stalls are open and busy, gives you the most to photograph.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the blue-and-white maypole in the middle of the market. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low so the maypole and stalls fit over your shoulder. Back-up plan: the Karl Valentin fountain, a playful backdrop that's also inside the market.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower has an entrance fee, so check the official site before you go. If you want to photograph people up close, ask first. The maypole may not be in place, and parts of the market may be fenced off, so check when you arrive.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the market from the tower, then go down and find the exact stall row you were looking at from above.
card.good_to_know: The market was set up here by a decree of King Maximilian I in 1807. It began as a farmers' market and now has around 140 stalls and shops selling flowers, fruit, game, cheese, fish, spices and juices. Look out for the memorial fountains to Munich folk singers and comedians like Karl Valentin and Liesl Karlstadt.

card.hook: Picture a glass tornado with a roof that looks like a cloud resting on top. That's BMW Welt, and it's one of the easiest buildings in Munich to photograph, even on a small phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Lerchenauer Straße footbridge, on the Olympic Park side, and face west. The double cone is in front of you with the Olympic Tower rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the cone and the tower in one frame. Try 2x to make the tower bigger behind the building, and switch to 0.5x when you get close and want the whole cone and roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the cone on a lower third, and let the tower rise in the space behind it.
card.best_time: Come at blue hour, just after sunset. The sky still has some colour, and the cars on the road below leave light trails. For those, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing.
card.selfie_here: Use the bridge at BMW Welt that looks toward the double cone. Turn your back to the cone, use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone offers it), and let the 28-metre cone fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the footbridge to take your photo with the cone behind you, and check the framing on the spot, because this bridge is better known for building shots than people shots.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed throughout the public areas of BMW Welt. Personal photos are usually fine, but professional shoots or commercial use may need permission, so check any signs. Use the footbridge rather than crossing the busy road, and watch for traffic and other walkers while you frame your shot.
card.challenge: Get the cone and the Olympic Tower in one shot with the building's lines perfectly straight. No leaning allowed!
card.good_to_know: BMW Welt was designed by COOP HIMMELB(L)AU of Vienna. It was built between 2003 and 2007 and opened on 17 October 2007. The roof carries a large solar installation, and the building is described as the most visited tourist attraction in Bavaria.

card.hook: You could stroll right past this one on Sendlinger Straße, and plenty of people do. Then you spot a curved, colourful front squeezed between two houses and think, wait, what is that?
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement of Sendlinger Straße on the opposite side of the street from the church, at the phone icon on the map. Face the portal straight on, with the neighbouring houses on either side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and both neighbouring houses, since the street is narrow. Switch to 1x for a straighter look at the portal, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the columns and figures above the door.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the portal up with the centre of the frame so the curved front looks nicely balanced.
card.best_time: You can shoot the outside from the pavement at any time. Just avoid church services if you want to see inside, because sightseeing isn't possible then.

One visitor mentions a fence keeping you from getting close, so step back from the wall. No page describes an exact selfie spot, so pick your own and check the framing on screen.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep the flash off inside, as it can disturb worshippers and other visitors. Photography rules inside may vary, so check when you arrive.
card.challenge: Get one frame of the whole front with both neighbouring houses, then one close-up of the figures above the door, and see if you can tell they belong to the same church.
card.good_to_know: The Asam brothers built this church between 1733 and 1746 as their own private church. Egid Quirin was a sculptor and Cosmas Damian a painter, and the plot is only about 22 by 8 metres. The choir was badly damaged in a bomb attack in 1944 and restored between 1975 and 1983.

card.good_to_know: The island was once called Kohleninsel (coal island). It became Museumsinsel when the city gave it to the museum in 1903. Before 1772 nothing was built there because the river flooded it so often. The permanent building opened on 2 May 1925, and bombing had damaged about 80% of the buildings by the end of 1944.

card.hook: Picture a park so big that Munich shrinks to a thin line of towers on the horizon. That's the view from the little hill in the English Garden, and it feels a bit like cheating.
card.stand_here: Head up to the Monopteros, the round temple on the artificial hill, and stand on its platform or on the grass slope just below. Face out over the meadows and treetops towards the towers of central Munich, including the Frauenkirche.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the meadow, the trees and the faraway towers all in one go. Then try 2x to pull the Frauenkirche and its neighbours closer (higher zooms depend on your phone). Use zoom 0.5x when you want the temple and the sweep of the slope.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower third line and let the green meadow fill the bottom of the picture.
card.best_time: Go in the golden hour before sunset. In summer, arrive 30 to 45 minutes early so you get a good spot on the slope.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Monopteros on top of the hill, reached by the spiral path up. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the temple over your shoulder, so the green park and the towers sneak in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near the Japanese Tea House to take a photo that frames the Monopteros hill across the park, but check the Tea House spot on your map first.
card.rules_and_safety: The Monopteros is an open-air public place, but check the official site for current conditions and any entry fee. If you visit the Eisbach wave, remember one guide warns the currents can be dangerous, so it's only for experienced surfers.
card.challenge: Take three frames at zoom 0.5x, 1x and 2x, then pick your winner. Bonus points if the skyline stays perfectly level.
card.good_to_know: The English Garden covers about 3.7 square kilometres, which makes it one of the world's largest city parks. Work began in 1789 for Elector Charles Theodore, and it opened to the public in 1792. The hill was added later by Carl August Sckell, and the temple was damaged by bombing in the Second World War.

card.hook: Most people march straight to the huge palace front, but you're about to sit on a lakeside bench with a little pavilion and still water, and it's usually far quieter than the forecourt.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lakeside in the southern part of the park, facing the small Badenburg pavilion across the water. The palace lies about 800 m to the north-east in a straight line.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the pavilion and its lake together. Go to 2x to pick out the pavilion's details and its reflection, or drop to 0.5x if you want the whole lakeside with the benches and trees.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pavilion, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the pavilion and the water. The lakeside also tends to be calmer outside the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Walk on to the wide gravel square in front of the palace's main façade, use your front camera and let the palace rise behind your shoulder. For a different look, try the broad staircase at the back of the palace, facing the park with the palace at your back (that one comes from a single guide, so don't be surprised if it takes a minute to find).
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small bridge over the central canal, facing the palace along the water, while you stand on the canal path in front of them with the palace in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Some park paths are gravel or grass and can be slippery after rain. The park is public, but opening hours change with the season and the palace interior is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a bench or an overhanging branch to sit in the foreground of your shot, then wait for the water to go still so the pavilion's reflection comes out clean.
card.good_to_know: Nymphenburg was commissioned in 1664 by Ferdinand Maria and Henriette Adelaide of Savoy, and the central pavilion was finished in 1675. The whole frontage is about 632 m wide, which is wider than Versailles. The park opened to the public in 1792, and King Ludwig II was born here in 1845.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the lakeside in the southern part of the park, facing the small Badenburg pavilion across the water. The palace lies about 800 m to the north-east in a straight line.

card.hook: Tip your head back and keep going, because this building doesn't stop. Brick, limestone, pointed gables and carved detail run from the ground right up to a tower with a tiny figure on top.
card.stand_here: Stand in Marienplatz, in front of the Mariensäule (the Marian Column), and face the north façade of the New Town Hall. It's to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot from Marienplatz.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade and tower in one frame. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the tower top and the statues. Use 1x for the column with the Town Hall behind it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the façade and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet, when the square is quieter and the light is softer. It gets crowded around the Glockenspiel times, including 11am and 12pm.
card.selfie_here: Hold the front camera a bit higher than your face, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and turn so the landmark sits over your shoulder. Take a few, because crowds wander into the back of your shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Going up the Town Hall tower or Alter Peter is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a Live Photo at 11am or 12pm and see if you can catch the Glockenspiel figures mid-move.
card.good_to_know: The first section of the New Town Hall was built between 1867 and 1874 to a design by Georg Hauberrisser, and the tower was added between 1898 and 1905. The main façade is almost 100 metres long and carries statues of Henry the Lion and nearly the whole line of the Wittelsbach rulers of Bavaria, the largest princely cycle on a German town hall. The tower is 85 metres high and topped by the Münchner Kindl figure.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Marienplatz, in front of the Mariensäule (the Marian Column), and face the north façade of the New Town Hall. It's to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot from Marienplatz.

card.hook: Old Peter pokes up above the Munich rooftops like he's keeping an eye on everyone's lunch plans. Spot him from the street and you'll want to get him in the shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Sankt-Jacobs-Platz and face north-east, because that's where the church lies. You'll see the facade and tower together, with the Rindermarkt side of the building in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the facade and the whole height of the tower. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the steeple top and the tower details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer on the streets around the church. Light from the side shows off the stonework better than flat midday light.
card.selfie_here: Try the Petersplatz, the square in front of the church. Stand with your back to the church and face down toward the Viktualienmarkt, then use the front camera at 0.5x so the tower can sneak in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Viktualienmarkt street facing the church, so they have the tower in frame while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, and the tower may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go. Going up the tower means climbing lots of stairs, which can be tough if you have mobility issues or vertigo.
card.challenge: Get Old Peter standing perfectly straight on a gridline, with a market stall or a bit of street life tucked in below him.
card.good_to_know: St. Peter's is the oldest recorded parish church in Munich, and many people think the city began around it. A church stood here before the city was founded in 1158. The tower is 91 metres high, and its Renaissance steeple top was added in the early 17th century.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Sankt-Jacobs-Platz and face north-east, because that's where the church lies. You'll see the facade and tower together, with the Rindermarkt side of the building in view.

card.hook: Walk up the Glyptothek steps and Königsplatz opens out below you like a giant, very tidy lawn, with a stone gate waiting at the far end. It's one of those rare spots where the whole scene is already lined up for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Glyptothek steps and face across the square toward the Propyläen gate. The middle of the square lies to the south-west of you, and the museum's own columns frame the edge of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x on the steps to fit the columns, the square and lots of sky into one picture. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the Propyläen, and try 2x if you want the gate all to itself.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the Propyläen on one of the vertical lines and keep the horizon level so the buildings stand up straight.
card.best_time: The steps are a sunny spot, so a bright day suits them. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
card.selfie_here: Try the open gravel in the middle of the square, in front of the Staatliche Antikensammlungen, where the neoclassical facades fill the frame behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a little low so you get more building and sky.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Brienner Straße at its east end, on the Propyläen approach, and shoot west toward the gate so the whole thing fits, while you stand in the square in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The Propyläen can't be walked through, and it now stands on a traffic island, so stick to the pavements and stay out of the roadway. The square often hosts concerts and public gatherings, so check ahead for events, and a commercial shoot may need permission.
card.challenge: Get the Propyläen sitting perfectly on a grid line with a dead-level horizon, then see if a friend can spot the difference from your first try.
card.good_to_know: The three main buildings went up between 1816 and 1845, and Leo von Klenze designed both the Glyptothek and the gate. The middle of the square sits almost a metre lower than its edges, which makes the buildings look taller. That's why the pictures come out so symmetrical, with plenty of sky.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Glyptothek steps and face across the square toward the Propyläen gate. The middle of the square lies to the south-west of you, and the museum's own columns frame the edge of your shot.

card.hook: Most people photograph the Chinese Tower from inside the beer garden, with a sea of tables in front. You're going to skip the queue and look back at it from a hill, like a postcard.
card.stand_here: Climb to the hilltop terrace of the Monopteros temple. Face north, because the Chinese Tower sits that way, across the park.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the big view over the meadows and treetops. Try 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of the park, then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is washed out so it keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Golden hour and sunset are the best. Weekends are fun too, since brass bands play, and in winter the Christmas market adds people and colour.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the beer garden benches around the base of the tower and sit with it behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the tower over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower's inside is closed to the public, so all your pictures will be taken from outside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, one zoomed shot of just the tower, and then see if you can spot the old town steeples on a clear day.
card.good_to_know: The Chinese Tower is a wooden, pagoda-style tower that rises above the tables and trees of a busy Bavarian beer garden. It's one of Munich's best-loved beer-garden landmarks. The Monopteros viewpoint is free, and so is entering the beer garden, but check the official site for events or changes before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Climb to the hilltop terrace of the Monopteros temple. Face north, because the Chinese Tower sits that way, across the park.

card.hook: Imagine a giant see-through tent thrown over a park, with a lake at its feet and a hill made for lounging. That's Olympiapark, and the view from the hill is the one you'll want to remember.
card.stand_here: Head to the top of the Olympiaberg, the grassy hill on the south side of the park. Face south-west, looking across the tent roof toward the Alps.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the whole scene, then go to 1x for a tidier frame. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tent roof or the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, with a bit of grass in the bottom corner for depth.
card.best_time: Sunset is the favourite, with golden light on the roof and the lake. The Alps show up best on cold, dry days after a front has passed.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the shore of the Olympiasee with your back to the water, using the front camera, so the Olympiaturm sits over your shoulder and in the reflection. Try 0.5x if you want more of the scene in.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the grass mound on the lake side, where the tent roofs, the tower and the water all fit in one frame, while you pose in the view.
card.rules_and_safety: The Olympiaturm is closed for renovation and the stadium interior is closed for some years, so plan on exterior views only. The hill needs no ticket, but check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: On a calm day, catch the tower's reflection in the lake and see if you can get the tent roof's curves in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Olympiapark was built for the 1972 Summer Olympics on the old Oberwiesenfeld airfield. The tent roof was designed by Frei Otto with Günter Behnisch, and the landscaping was by Günther Grzimek. It's still a public park, and people have sat on the hill to listen to stadium concerts for free.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the top of the Olympiaberg, the grassy hill on the south side of the park. Face south-west, looking across the tent roof toward the Alps.

card.hook: Two stone lions, three arches and a big open square: the Feldherrnhalle practically poses for you. Your only job is to get far enough back to fit it all in.
card.stand_here: Head for Odeonsplatz: the Feldherrnhalle is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east. Stand in the open part of the square and face south-east towards the loggia.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the whole loggia with its three arches and the square around it. If you walk closer and it won't fit, tap zoom 0.5x. Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the lions or the statues.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the central arch with the middle of the frame so the loggia sits level, with a little open square in front to show its size.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon are the usual suggestions. At dusk, switch on night mode and hold your phone as still as you can against your body.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the steps between the two lions, face down Ludwigstraße and use the front camera, so the loggia is behind you. Or stand under the central arch facing south down Residenzstraße, where the view lines up with the Frauenkirche towers. Tap zoom 0.5x if you want more of the arches in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the steps of the Theatinerkirche and shoot back towards the loggia while you stand in front of it, so the whole facade fits in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Events, demonstrations, filming or building work can limit access to the loggia and the square, and scaffolding can block the view. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few shots a minute apart and see if you can catch one with no strangers wandering through the foreground.
card.good_to_know: King Ludwig I of Bavaria commissioned the Feldherrnhalle to honour the Bavarian Army. It was built between 1841 and 1844, modelled on the Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence. The two stone lions at the front date from 1906. It is also where the 1923 Beer Hall Putsch ended in a gun battle, so the site carries a heavy history as well as an architectural one.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Odeonsplatz: the Feldherrnhalle is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east. Stand in the open part of the square and face south-east towards the loggia.

card.hook: You can't miss this one: a buttery yellow church with twin towers and a big green dome, sitting right across from the Residence.
card.stand_here: Start at Odeonsplatz. The church is just to the south, about 1 minute on foot from there. Stand in the centre of the square and face the west side of the church, with the Feldherrnhalle and the Residence framing the view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole facade and the open square in one shot. Then try 1x for a tidier, less stretched look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the middle of the facade up with the centre line so the towers look even, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon or the hour before sunset, when the yellow glows. One guide suggests early on a Sunday morning if you want fewer people in the square.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Hofgarten and stand in front of the temple-like pavilion with the church behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x so the facade fits over your shoulder. One local guide says early morning gives the best backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Odeonsplatz and shoot towards the church, while you stand between them and the yellow facade.
card.rules_and_safety: If the Feldherrnhalle has scaffolding on it, keep it out of your frame. Photos inside the church are generally allowed, but flash is not.
card.challenge: Can you get both towers perfectly even, with the green dome peeking up and a nice slice of sky on top?
card.good_to_know: The church was built between 1663 and 1690. Elector Ferdinand Maria and his wife Henriette Adelaide of Savoy founded it to give thanks for the birth of their son, Max Emanuel. The towers are about 65 metres and the dome is 71 metres, and the Rococo facade you see today was finished in 1768.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at Odeonsplatz. The church is just to the south, about 1 minute on foot from there. Stand in the centre of the square and face the west side of the church, with the Feldherrnhalle and the Residence framing the view.

card.hook: Three towers, one big arch and a busy road: the Isartor looks like a gate a child would draw, and that's why it's such an easy first photo in Munich.
card.stand_here: Stand in Isartorplatz, across the road from the gate, and face west. The gate lies just to the north-west, so step back until the central tower and the arch both fit.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from the square. If the side towers get cut off, tap 0.5x. Save 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the painted fresco and the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the central tower up with a vertical line, with the arch in the middle, so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning means fewer people in your shot. In late afternoon the light on the front of the gate turns warmer. At Christmas-market time, stalls can block the view.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Tal side of the main tower and find the mirror-image clock. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the reversed clock face over your shoulder as a quirky backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Tal street facing the gate so the whole tower is in the frame, while you pose with the gate behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is a busy traffic junction, so wait for a gap and keep cars out of the shot. The museum, café and courtyard inside may have their own opening times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you spot the clock that runs backwards and squeeze it into your selfie with a straight face?
card.good_to_know: The Isartor was built in 1337 as part of Munich's second city wall, and the main tower is about 40 metres high. It's the most easterly of the city's three surviving Gothic town gates, alongside Sendlinger Tor and Karlstor. The fresco on the front, added in 1835, shows Emperor Louis returning in victory after the Battle of Mühldorf in 1322, and today the gate also houses a museum for the comedian Karl Valentin, with a café.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Isartorplatz, across the road from the gate, and face west. The gate lies just to the north-west, so step back until the central tower and the arch both fit.

card.hook: Picture a long, straight boulevard with a giant three-arched gate waiting at the end of it, and a statue on top driving a chariot pulled by lions. That's the Siegestor, and the street does half the work of lining up your photo for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ludwigstraße, south of the arch, and face north so the gate sits in the middle of your frame at the end of the street. Keep the street running straight up to it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole arch, centred. Try 0.5x if you want more boulevard and sky, or if you walk up closer to the gate.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the arch up with the centre line, and keep your phone level so the pillars don't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is lovely. Very late at night the streets are quieter, so fewer cars creep into your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the narrow pedestrian islands just north or south of the gate, or right under the middle of the central arch, with the gate over your shoulder. Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x to fit more of the monument in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Ludwigstraße at the southern end of the approach and shoot north, so the arch sits centred behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate sits on a busy road, so take extra care when stepping up to or under the arch for photos, and watch the traffic.
card.challenge: Can you get the lions pulling the chariot and the Bavaria statue in the same frame, with no car sneaking in? Good luck, and be patient.
card.good_to_know: King Ludwig I commissioned the gate. Friedrich von Gärtner designed it, and Eduard Mezger completed it in 1852. After heavy war damage it was only partly restored, and the inscription on the back now reads "Dem Sieg geweiht, vom Krieg zerstört, zum Frieden mahnend" ("Dedicated to victory, destroyed by war, urging peace").
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ludwigstraße, south of the arch, and face north so the gate sits in the middle of your frame at the end of the street. Keep the street running straight up to it.

card.hook: Karlstor looks like a castle gate that wandered into a busy junction and decided to stay. The pointed towers and the arch make a simple, strong shape, so even a quick snap looks good.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of Karlsplatz (Stachus) and face the gate, with the square's fountain low in front of you. The gate is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the fountain and both towers fit in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the gate alone, or 2x to pick out the towers without stepping into the traffic.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the arch in the middle, then tap the gate and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late evening is quietest, and the light is softer too. In the evening, try night mode and hold your phone steady against a wall or railing.
card.selfie_here: Walk a few steps through the arch onto Neuhauser Straße, turn so your back is to the gate, and let the arch frame you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more of the gate over your shoulder. Or stand at the Stachus fountain with the gate behind you, though one visitor found the fountain switched off.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in the middle of Karlsplatz, facing the gate, so the fountain and the arch both fit in the frame while you pose near the fountain with the arch behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Karlsplatz is a busy junction, so watch the traffic when you step back for a shot. The arch is an open public passage, but check the official site before you go in case of works or events.
card.challenge: Can you get the fountain, the arch and both pointed towers in one shot without a stranger's head sneaking in? Good luck, it's a busy gate.
card.good_to_know: Karlstor was first mentioned in 1302 and was called Neuhauser Tor until 1791, when it was renamed after the Elector, Charles Theodore. It's one of three medieval gates still standing in Munich. The two towers were reworked in Neo-Gothic style in 1861/62 and later built into the curved buildings on either side, finished in 1902.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of Karlsplatz (Stachus) and face the gate, with the square's fountain low in front of you. The gate is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot.
